# 2 Kings Chapter 24 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 244v–245r

---

**1** During Jehoiakim's reign, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon invaded the land. Jehoiakim submitted to him for three years, then rebelled.

**2** The LORD sent raiding bands of Babylonians, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites against Judah to destroy it, just as the LORD had warned through his prophets.

**3** These disasters came upon Judah at the LORD's command, to banish them from his presence because of the sins Manasseh had committed —

**4** including all the innocent blood he had shed. He had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD would not forgive.

**5** The rest of Jehoiakim's reign is recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.

**6** Jehoiakim died, and his son Jehoiachin succeeded him.

**7** The king of Egypt never marched out of his own country again, because the king of Babylon had seized everything that had belonged to Egypt, from the Brook of Egypt all the way to the Euphrates River.

**8** Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem.

**9** He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just as his father had done.

**10** During his reign, the officers of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon marched against Jerusalem and laid siege to it.

**11** Nebuchadnezzar himself arrived at the city while his officers were besieging it.

**12** King Jehoiachin of Judah, along with his mother, his attendants, his nobles, and his officials, surrendered to the king of Babylon. The king of Babylon took him prisoner — it was the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign.

**13** Nebuchadnezzar carried off all the treasures from the LORD's temple and the royal palace. He cut up all the gold articles that King Solomon had made for the LORD's temple — just as the LORD had predicted.

**14** He deported all of Jerusalem: all the commanders, all the soldiers — ten thousand captives in all — plus every skilled craftsman and metalworker. Only the poorest people were left in the land.

**15** He took Jehoiachin to Babylon as a prisoner, along with the king's mother, his wives, his officials, and the leading citizens of the land — all taken into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.

**16** The king of Babylon also deported seven thousand soldiers and one thousand craftsmen and metalworkers — all strong and ready for battle.

**17** Then the king of Babylon installed Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah as king and changed his name to Zedekiah.

**18** Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.

**19** He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just as Jehoiakim had done.

**20** All this happened because of the LORD's anger against Jerusalem and Judah — anger so fierce that he finally banished them from his presence. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — The beginning of the end:** Nebuchadnezzar's arrival marks the irreversible shift. Judah is now caught between two empires — Egypt (whose influence has collapsed, v.7) and Babylon. Jehoiakim's rebellion after three years of vassalage triggers the chain of events that leads to destruction.

**Verse 4 — "the LORD would not forgive":** This is the narrator's final verdict on Manasseh's legacy. No amount of Josiah's reform, no amount of national repentance, can reverse the judgment. The innocent blood cries out, and God refuses to silence it. This is not a statement about divine caprice but about the irreversibility of certain moral thresholds.

**Verse 12 — The first deportation (597 BCE):** Jehoiachin's surrender is pragmatic — he spares the city from destruction, at least for now. But the deportation strips Judah of its military, artisan, and administrative classes. What remains is an empty shell ruled by a puppet king.

**Verse 20 — Zedekiah's rebellion:** The chapter ends with the fatal act. Zedekiah, a puppet installed by Babylon, rebels against his overlord. The narrator frames this as divine orchestration: God's anger drives events toward their terrible conclusion.

*— PNEUMA*
